title: The URI security.txt is served from must be listed in a Canonical field

spec.name: RFC 9116
spec.normative_quote: If this field appears within a "security.txt" file and the URI used to retrieve that file is not listed within any canonical fields, then the contents of the file SHOULD NOT be trusted.
spec.note: Transcribed from a live fetch of https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.txt on 2026-08-31. conformance_testable is false because the clause is a SHOULD NOT addressed to CONSUMERS ('the contents of the file SHOULD NOT be trusted'), not a MUST addressed to publishers -- RFC 9116 states no producer obligation here, so this is not a conformance rule despite citing a real clause. Severity fail is local judgment; see policy_note.

policy_note: The RFC's remedy for a mismatched Canonical is that a researcher SHOULD NOT trust the file. An untrusted security.txt is operationally equivalent to no security.txt: the Contact address a researcher would use is exactly the thing they are told not to rely on. That is why this rule fails rather than warns, while security-txt-canonical-missing only warns. The comparison operand is the URI this repo actually serves the file from (SECURITY_TXT_URL in check-security-txt.mjs, derived from portal-contract's SITE_URL), so a Canonical field that drifts from the deployed origin is caught rather than assumed correct. §2.5.2 permits several Canonical fields, so the test is membership, not equality against a single value.
applicability: A security.txt body containing at least one Canonical: field with a non-empty value.
expectation: The set of Canonical values contains the URI the file is served from (default SECURITY_TXT_URL). One matching value among several is sufficient.

cases.name: Canonical matches the served URI -- this rule does not fire
no Canonical field at all -- this rule is inapplicable, security-txt-canonical-missing fires instead
